Charisma

kuh-RIZ-muh -- from a Greek word meaning a gift of grace. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Charisma is a compelling attractiveness or charm that can inspire devotion in others.

Even strangers found themselves captivated by the young senator's charisma the moment she began to speak.

Worked Example

A new coach walks into a struggling locker room, and within a single speech, every player is sitting up straighter, ready to run through a wall for her.

That magnetic personal charm that draws people in and inspires loyalty is exactly what charisma describes. Unlike 'skill,' which is a learned ability, charisma is a compelling quality of personality.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

charm: a quality of attracting and delighting others

magnetism: a powerful attractiveness that draws others in

allure: the power to attract, tempt, or delight

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

dullness: a lack of interest or excitement

awkwardness: a lack of grace or ease in manner

Where it sits · how strongly it pulls people in — charm → charisma → magnetism

charm vs. charisma: Charm is a more everyday word than charisma -- charm can describe any pleasant, likable quality, while charisma specifically implies a powerful presence that inspires real devotion in others.

magnetism vs. charisma: Magnetism can feel even stronger than charisma: charisma describes a charming, inspiring personal quality, while magnetism suggests people are almost irresistibly pulled toward that person.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — -charis-

root — -charis-: grace, favor, gift (Greek (charis))

suffix — -ma

suffix — -ma: Greek noun ending; the result of (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: Greek charis meant 'grace, favor, gift,' and the Greek noun ending -ma names the result -- so charisma is literally 'a gift of grace,' a personal quality that feels almost given rather than earned. The same root gives us charity.
